title: Love has boundaries
hook: love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed

segments.voice: Yesterday, love unreturned, and Leah turning from hoping to praise. Your line was still love. Did you manage to call an old love by its real name? Today, love that knows where it ends. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

People were coming and going, more of them than anyone could greet. In the Gospel of Mark, the disciples have just come back and told Jesus all they had done and taught, and the place is so busy, the text says, that they had no leisure so much as to eat. Nobody would blame a teacher for saying keep going, there's more to do. Instead Jesus says something else, and it's worth hearing on a day when the phone keeps buzzing and someone always needs one more thing. Today: love has boundaries.
screen: `COMING AND GOING.` → `NO LEISURE SO MUCH AS TO EAT.` → `JESUS SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James text Jesus tells them: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Apart. Rest. In the middle of real need, with real people waiting. The Gospel doesn't treat this as a failure of love. It treats it as part of the work. Second, his own habit. Luke's Gospel says, in a short line, "he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." The same teacher who healed and fed and taught also walked away from the crowd, on purpose. Christians read this in more than one way, but the plain picture is a person whose love had a shape, with edges, with times of being unavailable. Third, the harder edge. When Jesus sends his followers out, Matthew's Gospel has him tell them that where a house or a city won't receive them, they should leave, and shake off the dust of their feet. Not fight. Not stay and be ground down. Leave, and keep the peace inside. Some readers find a principle in it: you can wish someone well and still walk out of their door. Fourth, what this means on an ordinary day. Love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed. A boundary isn't a wall to punish someone. It's a line that tells the truth about what you can carry. Saying no to one thing can be the way you keep saying yes to the people you love. And if anyone listening is in a situation where love is being used to hurt them, a boundary may mean getting help from someone you trust. That too can be love, including love for yourself.
screen: `COME APART, AND REST A WHILE.` · `HE WITHDREW HIMSELF, AND PRAYED.` · `SHAKE OFF THE DUST.` · `A LINE THAT TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `LOVE HAS BOUNDARIES.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop. Breathe in, and feel where your body ends: your skin, the chair under you, the floor under your feet. That edge isn't unkind. It's just where you are. Now bring to mind one place in your life where a healthy boundary is needed. A time of day, a kind of request, a conversation that keeps going wrong. Don't plan a speech. Just let one clear sentence form, something simple you could say. Hold it gently, without anger. If you pray, you can ask for courage in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Desert place. Where Jesus told his disciples to come apart and rest, even while the crowds still needed them. Today's word.
Your line: love has edges. Today, keep one healthy boundary kindly: a no said warmly, a phone set face down, a rest you don't apologize for. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians often point to the Gospel scenes where Jesus withdraws to pray as a pattern for rest and retreat, and people on many paths keep a sabbath, a quiet hour or a retreat as a protected time apart.

trapdoor: what you thought: real love never says no.
what it means: love has a shape, with rest, time apart and lines it won't cross, and it doesn't require being harmed.
what a scholar hears: Mark 6:31's rest a while, Luke 5:16's withdrawing to pray, and Matthew 10:14's shaking off the dust, read together as love with edges.
